Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Ten people were killed Tuesday when a gunman rampaged through a Finnish college, police officials said. Officials say Matti Juhani Saari began firing in a classroom at the college before shooting himself. Over the course of 90 minutes, Saari fired a few shots at police, Finnish broadcaster YLE said. Jukka Forsberg, a maintenance worker at the school, told YLE that the gunman was wearing a ski mask and walked into the building with a large bag. About 150 students were on campus Kauhajoki city's School of Hospitality in southwestern Finland. Forsberg said, "I heard several dozen rounds of shots. In other words, it was an automatic pistol. I saw some female students who were wailing and moaning, and one managed to escape out the back door." Smoke billowed from a building on campus, but officials could not immediately say what caused the fire.  Watch pictures from the scene » . Tapio Varmola, who was visiting the school at the time, told CNN he was in a building about two blocks away when the shootings occurred. After the shootings, he said, he heard students shouting. Police came about 10 minutes after they were called, Varmola said. "It took two hours to get this situation ended," he said. Saari, 22, died Tuesday afternoon from a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head at Tampere University Hospital, said medical director Matti Lehto. At least one other person suffered serious injuries in the shooting, he added. Police had interviewed and released Saari on Monday after he posted violent videos on YouTube, authorities said. As Saari did not directly threaten anyone in the videos, there were no grounds for further action, national police Commissioner Mikko Paatero told YLE. Authorities learned about the videos Friday but could not reach Saari until Monday, Paatero told YLE. Police also searched his home, YLE reported. Four videos of a man firing a pistol at a shooting range were posted by a "Mr. Saari" from Kauhajoki, where the college is based, according to his YouTube profile. The profile also included a video tribute to the Columbine High School shooters, Eric Harris and Dylan Klebold, at the top of the man's favorites list. The videos were posted over a three-week period this month. None was posted in the last week.  Watch more about the YouTube videos » . The account was suspended within hours of the shooting, which began about 11 a.m. local time (0800 GMT). MTV-3's Foreign Editor Risto Puolimatka told CNN that Saari was also issued with a temporary gun license last month. It was the gunman's first license, Puolimatka said. Finnish President Tarja Halonen expressed her condolences from the United Nations, where she is attending the annual General Assembly. She also commented on the YouTube videos. "We, parents and elderly people, have a little bit of feeling about the Internet," she said at an impromptu TV interview. "It's like a strange planet for us. But it's not so. It's part of our world, so we have to step in." She praised efforts by police, who she said "were already on board" by interviewing Saari. Authorities hoped that was enough to take care of any threat, but "now we see that it was not," she said. The school taught late teens and young adults, Jarkko Sipila of MTV 3 told CNN. "It's more or less like an agricultural or professional school where people teach how to make food or how to cook in big kitchen, in industrial kitchens," he said. Kauhajoki, with a population of about 15,000, is about 290km (180 miles) from the capital, Helsinki. The incident comes almost a year after another school shooting left nine people, including the gunman, dead in the Finnish town of Tuusala. Before that shooting, the gunman, 18-year-old student Pekka-Eric Auvinen, posted a video on YouTube titled "Jokela High School Massacre 11/7/2007," identifying the date and location of the attack. "All these memories are being brought back and people are asking the question, 'Why again?' " Sipila said. Finland enjoys a strong tradition of hunting and has a high proportion of gun ownership, with 2 million firearms owned in a nation of 5 million people.

# Finland Rocked by Deadly Shooting at Vocational College

(CNN) -- A gunman's rampage through a Finnish college left ten people dead on Tuesday, according to police officials.

Authorities report that Matti Juhani Saari opened fire in a classroom before turning the weapon on himself. According to Finnish broadcaster YLE, the shooter exchanged sporadic gunfire with police during a 90-minute standoff.

Jukka Forsberg, who works in maintenance at the school, described to YLE how the attacker entered wearing a ski mask and carrying a large bag. Approximately 150 students were present at the School of Hospitality in Kauhajoki, a city in southwestern Finland, when the attack unfolded.

"I heard several dozen rounds of shots. In other words, it was an automatic pistol," Forsberg recounted. "I saw some female students who were wailing and moaning, and one managed to escape out the back door."

Smoke was seen pouring from one of the campus buildings, though the cause of the fire remained unclear to officials.

Tapio Varmola, who happened to be visiting the school when the violence broke out, was in a building roughly two blocks away. He told CNN that following the gunfire, he could hear students crying out. Police arrived approximately ten minutes after being alerted, he noted, adding, "It took two hours to get this situation ended."

Medical director Matti Lehto of Tampere University Hospital confirmed that the 22-year-old Saari succumbed Tuesday afternoon to a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head. Lehto also noted that at least one additional victim sustained serious injuries.

## Prior Police Contact

Authorities revealed that Saari had been questioned by police and subsequently released just one day before the massacre, after he had uploaded violent footage to YouTube. National Police Commissioner Mikko Paatero explained to YLE that because Saari made no direct threats in the videos, there was insufficient justification for further intervention.

Paatero indicated that police first became aware of the videos on Friday, yet were unable to make contact with Saari until Monday. YLE also reported that officers had searched his residence.

According to his YouTube profile, a user identified as "Mr. Saari" from Kauhajoki had uploaded four clips showing a man shooting a pistol at a firing range over a three-week span this month, with the most recent posting occurring more than a week prior to the attack. Notably, a tribute video honoring Columbine shooters Eric Harris and Dylan Klebold topped his list of favorites. His account was deactivated within hours of the shooting, which commenced around 11 a.m. local time (0800 GMT).

MTV-3's Foreign Editor Risto Puolimatka informed CNN that Saari had received his first-ever temporary firearms license just the previous month.

## Presidential Response

Speaking from the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Finnish President Tarja Halonen offered condolences while also addressing the role of the YouTube videos.

"We, parents and elderly people, have a little bit of feeling about the Internet," she remarked during an unplanned television interview. "It's like a strange planet for us. But it's not so. It's part of our world, so we have to step in."

She commended police for having already questioned Saari, noting that authorities believed this action might have neutralized any danger. "Now we see that it was not" enough, she acknowledged.

## About the School and Region

Jarkko Sipila of MTV 3 described the institution to CNN as catering to older teenagers and young adults, comparing it to "an agricultural or professional school where people teach how to make food or how to cook in big kitchens, in industrial kitchens."

Kauhajoki, home to roughly 15,000 residents, sits about 290 kilometers (180 miles) from Helsinki, the nation's capital.

## Echoes of Previous Tragedy

This attack arrives nearly one year after a similar tragedy claimed nine lives, including the shooter's, in the town of Tuusala. That gunman, 18-year-old student Pekka-Eric Auvinen, had likewise posted a YouTube video beforehand—one titled "Jokela High School Massacre 11/7/2007"—which named both the date and site of his planned attack.

"All these memories are being brought back and people are asking the question, 'Why again?'" Sipila reflected.

Finland maintains deep-rooted hunting traditions and correspondingly high rates of gun ownership, with an estimated 2 million firearms in circulation among its population of roughly 5 million.

# The Kauhajoki School Shooting: A Tragedy That Could Have Been Prevented

On September 23, 2008, a 22-year-old student named Matti Juhani Saari carried out one of the deadliest mass shootings in Finnish history, killing ten people at a vocational college in the small western town of Kauhajoki before turning the gun on himself. The attack shocked the nation and raised serious questions about missed warning signs that, in hindsight, might have prevented the tragedy.

## The Attack Unfolds

Saari entered a classroom at the Kauhajoki School of Hospitality and opened fire on students and staff without warning. What followed was a prolonged and harrowing standoff with law enforcement that stretched on for approximately 90 minutes. As police attempted to contain the situation and negotiate an end to the violence, Saari continued exchanging gunfire with responding officers. The confrontation ultimately ended when Saari turned his weapon on himself, dying from a self-inflicted gunshot wound rather than surrendering to authorities.

## Eyewitness Accounts of Chaos

Survivors and witnesses who managed to escape the building described a scene of sheer terror. The gunman was seen wearing a ski mask to conceal his identity and carrying a large bag—later revealed to contain additional ammunition and supplies for his assault. Those inside the school reported hearing dozens of rounds of automatic gunfire echoing through the hallways, sending students and faculty into a panicked scramble to find safety. Many fled the building in fear for their lives, while others barricaded themselves in rooms, uncertain of what was happening or how many attackers might be involved.

## Warning Signs Missed by Authorities

In the aftermath of the shooting, disturbing details emerged about Saari's activities in the days leading up to the attack. Astonishingly, police had already interviewed Saari just one day before he carried out his rampage. This interview was prompted by videos he had posted on YouTube showing himself firing a pistol at a shooting range—footage that displayed clear violent undertones. Despite these red flags, officers made the decision to release him, reasoning that he had not made any explicit or direct threats against specific individuals or the school itself.

## A Troubling Timeline

The timeline of events surrounding the discovery of these videos only deepened concerns about institutional failures. Authorities first became aware of Saari's disturbing online content on a Friday, several days before the attack took place. However, law enforcement officials reported that they were unable to make contact with Saari until the following Monday—the same day he ultimately carried out the shooting. This gap in communication and response time later became a focal point of scrutiny, as critics questioned whether swifter action might have altered the outcome.

## Additional Chaos: A Mysterious Fire

Compounding the tragedy, a fire broke out in one of the campus buildings during the course of the incident. The exact cause of the blaze was not immediately determined, adding another layer of confusion and danger to an already chaotic scene. Emergency responders were forced to contend not only with an active shooter situation but also with the added complication of fire suppression, further complicating rescue and evacuation efforts for those trapped inside.

## Aftermath and Legacy

The Kauhajoki shooting stands as a stark reminder of the challenges law enforcement faces in identifying and acting upon warning signs before they escalate into violence. The decision to release Saari despite his alarming online behavior sparked national debate about protocols for handling individuals who display concerning behavior without making explicit threats. The tragedy prompted Finland to reexamine its approach to gun control, mental health intervention, and the assessment of online content as a potential indicator of impending violence.

On September 23, 2008, a 22-year-old culinary student named Matti Juhani Saari walked into the Kauhajoki School of Hospitality in western Finland carrying a semi-automatic pistol and several bags of ammunition. What unfolded over the next hour and a half would become one of the deadliest school shootings in Finnish history and spark a national conversation about missed warning signs, gun control, and the failures of law enforcement to act on clear evidence of danger.

## The Attack

Saari entered the vocational school building and began shooting indiscriminately at students and staff. He then set fire to the building, trapping victims inside as emergency responders scrambled to reach the scene. Police arrived quickly, but a tense 90-minute standoff ensued as officers worked to secure the building and confront the gunman. When police finally closed in, Saari turned the gun on himself rather than surrender, ending the standoff but leaving behind a scene of devastation.

By the time the smoke cleared, ten people were confirmed dead, including students and a teacher. At least one other person suffered serious injuries in the attack, adding to the toll of a community left reeling from the violence.

## Warning Signs Ignored

Perhaps the most troubling aspect of the Kauhajoki shooting was the revelation that authorities had been alerted to Saari's disturbing behavior just one day before the attack. Saari had posted violent videos to YouTube, some of which appeared to foreshadow the very violence he would commit. These videos raised enough concern that police brought him in for questioning.

## Aftermath and Scrutiny

In the wake of the shooting, intense scrutiny fell on Finnish police and the systems in place for identifying and responding to potential threats. Critics questioned how someone who had displayed such alarming behavior online, and who had already come to the attention of law enforcement, could still have access to a firearm and the freedom to act on his violent impulses.

The Kauhajoki shooting came just under a year after a similar attack at Jokela High School in Finland, further intensifying calls for reform. # Gunman Kills 10 in Finnish School Shooting

**KAUHAJOKI, Finland** — A gunman opened fire at a vocational college in western Finland on Tuesday, killing at least nine students and staff members before turning the gun on himself, marking the second deadly school shooting in the country in less than a year.

Police identified the shooter as Matti Juhani Saari, a 22-year-old student at the Kauhajoki School of Hospitality, where the attack took place. Authorities said Saari used a .22-caliber semi-automatic pistol, the same type of weapon used in a similar attack at a Finnish school in November 2007 that left eight people dead.

According to police, Saari entered the building during morning classes and began shooting, then reportedly set fire to the premises, complicating rescue efforts as emergency crews worked to evacuate students and extinguish flames.

Local and national police, along with emergency medical services, responded rapidly to the scene. SWAT-style units were deployed, and the surrounding area was cordoned off as officers went room to room searching for the gunman and any additional victims. Saari was found with a self-inflicted gunshot wound and later died from his injuries.

Investigators said Saari had posted disturbing videos online in the days before the attack, including footage of himself firing a weapon at a shooting range, set to music, raising questions about whether warning signs had been missed. Finnish police confirmed they had questioned Saari the day before the shooting after being alerted to the videos, but said they found insufficient legal grounds to confiscate his weapon or detain him at the time.

Finnish Prime Minister Matti Vanhanen addressed the nation following the attack, calling it a "great tragedy" for the small community of Kauhajoki and for Finland as a whole. He emphasized that authorities would review the circumstances leading up to the shooting, including gun licensing laws and the handling of online threats.

This is the second such tragedy to strike Finland in less than a year. In November 2007, an 18-year-old gunman killed eight people at Jokela High School before killing himself, an event that had already prompted national debate over gun control and mental health services for young people.

Finland has some of the highest rates of gun ownership in Europe, and Tuesday's shooting is expected to reignite scrutiny over the country's firearm laws, particularly the ease with which young people can obtain handguns for sport shooting purposes.

Grief counselors and crisis teams have been dispatched to Kauhajoki to assist survivors, families of victims, and the broader community as they come to terms with the attack. Flags were lowered to half-staff across the region as officials confirmed the scale of the tragedy.

The investigation into the shooting continues, with authorities working to determine a possible motive and to review Saari's background, mental health history, and online activity in the lead-up to the attack.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

# Kauhajoki School Shooting (September 23, 2008)

## Overview
On September 23, 2008, a mass shooting occurred at the Kauhajoki School of Hospitality in Kauhajoki, Finland. The gunman, a 22-year-old student named Matti Saari, killed 10 people (nine students and one teacher) before dying by suicide.

## The Attack
Saari entered the vocational school building armed with a semi-automatic pistol and set fires using firebombs, targeting a classroom where students were taking an exam. He shot multiple victims before police arrived. When confronted, he shot himself; he later died from his injuries in the hospital.

## Eyewitness Accounts
Survivors described chaotic and terrifying scenes:
- Students reported hearing gunshots and initially being confused about what was happening, with some believing it might be a drill.
- Witnesses described smoke and fire filling parts of the building as Saari used incendiary devices alongside the firearm.
- Some students managed to escape through windows or hide in locked rooms.
- Accounts described the shooter moving methodically, suggesting a level of premeditation.

## YouTube Activity
Prior to the attack, Saari had posted disturbing videos on YouTube under the username "Mr Saari." These included:
- Footage of him firing a handgun at a shooting range.
- Videos with ominous captions and references suggesting violent intent.
- Content that appeared to foreshadow the attack, drawing comparisons to earlier school shootings, including the Jokela school shooting that had occurred in Finland less than a year prior (November 2007).

The videos raised significant questions afterward about whether warning signs were missed, since some content had reportedly been flagged or noticed before the attack.

## Reactions from Finnish Officials
- Finnish authorities expressed shock that a second school shooting had occurred in the country within less than a year, prompting national soul-searching about gun laws and mental health screening.
- Officials noted that Saari had been questioned by police shortly before the attack (after his YouTube videos came to attention) but was released, as authorities did not find sufficient legal grounds to confiscate his weapon at that time.
- Then-Prime Minister Matti Vanhanen expressed condolences and stated the tragedy would require a thorough review of gun control policies.
- The events prompted debate over Finland's relatively permissive firearms laws, particularly regarding handgun licensing for young adults.
- Finnish police faced criticism for not acting more decisively after being alerted to Saari's online activity days before the shooting.

## Aftermath
The Kauhajoki shooting, coming so soon after the Jokela shooting, led to significant policy discussions in Finland regarding firearm licensing requirements, age restrictions, and the monitoring of online content indicating potential violence.
